items_missed: Never asked 'how are you today?' or any warm-up.

Availability never confirmed. The customer named Sunday the 20th and Nicole repeated it back — 'Sunday, the twentieth. Okay' — without ever saying whether Einstein has a truck that day. The customer left the call not knowing if the date he named is even available.
Additional rooms never asked — no garage, storage unit, balcony, or patio on either end of a two-bedroom-to-two-story-house move.
Special considerations never probed — no long walks, narrow hallways, tight turns.
Storage stops and additional stops never asked.

Access concerns only half-covered. The elevator came up because the customer raised it himself, and Nicole never asked about parking, loading dock, COI requirements at the apartment, or truck access at the McKinney house.

Moving-stressor question never asked — and this customer was signalling hard. 'We've just had people scratch things and mess things up' is a customer telling you where his anxiety lives, and it surfaced only in the final ninety seconds, dragged out of the insurance question, never invited.
No 'pricing is super simple' opener — 'let me go ahead and explain how our pricing works.'
Rate given as a team number only. '$202 per hour for two movers and one truck' never breaks down to $101 per mover per hour, which is the figure a customer comparison-shopping four movers needs.

The day-of-week discount was raised and then abandoned. She said 'we actually have different rates, depending on the day of the move. What is your preferred move date?' — got 'Sunday the twentieth' — and then never told him what the cheaper days are or what they cost. She opened a price lever, learned he had a preferred date, and closed the lever without ever showing him what flexibility was worth. That is worse than not mentioning it: he now knows a cheaper option exists and that he wasn't offered it.

No hidden fees pitch never delivered. 'There's only one thing outside of the hourly rate, which is a one time travel fee of $75' is close but it is the inverse — it names the one fee that exists rather than the list of fees that don't. No credit card fees, no fuel surcharge, no heavy-item fees, no assembly fees — none of it was said, on a call where the customer's entire posture was comparison shopping.

No Worries Damage Coverage was never volunteered — it surfaced only because the customer asked, as an afterthought, on his way off the phone ('Oh, also what's your insurance coverage?'). It was never named as No Worries Damage Coverage.

Meet Your Mover never mentioned. The customer said in plain words 'we've just had people scratch things and mess things up' — knowing the movers' names and faces before they arrive is the direct answer, and it was never offered.
On-Time Guarantee never mentioned.

Entire Clock section absent — 0/4. When the clock starts was never explained. The two-and-a-half-hour minimum was never mentioned. Fifteen-minute proration was never mentioned. No sense-check. This is a customer who was quoted $1,085 to $1,287 and has no idea when the meter starts running, whether drive time is billable, what happens if the job runs to six and a half hours, or what the floor is. Not one of the four bullets was covered.

The customer's explicit request was not fulfilled. He asked for two quotes — 'our apartment elevator is broken often. So, I would like a quote for how much it'll cost without an elevator and with an elevator' — and got one number. Nicole acknowledged it with 'I see, okay' and then built a single five-to-six hour estimate that never says which scenario it represents. He asked a direct question, twice-framed, and it went unanswered.
Additional stops never asked or factored into the estimate.
Walk distance never asked or factored.
Traffic never mentioned, on a stated forty-minute drive from downtown Dallas out to McKinney.
No equivalents or plain-language anchors used.

Save Your Ass speech entirely absent — 0/10. No prep framing, no consolidation examples, no 'take a carload,' no close. On a call where the customer's stated priority was speed ('Let's try and make a little bit faster') and the quote came back over a thousand dollars, the prep speech is the one thing that lowers his number without lowering the rate.

Entire Quote/Booking section absent — 0/11. No booking attempt of any kind. No deposit never mentioned. No email offered, no email address collected — after eight minutes of work she has no way to reach this lead at all. No bolded-list framing, no 'reply with any corrections,' no 'any other questions before I let you go?', no hours, no how-to-reach-us. The customer said 'I'll reach out if we decide to go with you guys' and the entire response was 'Okay, awesome.'
Customer's name used zero times. She asked for it in the first sentence — 'may I have your name?' — got 'hunter Riley,' and never used it once across eight minutes.

No real farewell or save attempt. The customer said 'we probably won't go with you but this was good information,' which is a soft no with the door still open, and the reply was 'You're welcome. Thank you as well for considering.' No 'before you go, can I ask what you're comparing us against?', no 'let me at least email you the quote so you have it,' no attempt to keep the lead alive.

The insurance explanation collapsed at the decisive moment. The customer asked, reasonably, what repair actually means — 'what about the repair piece of it? What do you guys typically try and repair?' — and the answer was 'For repair. Sorry I think I can ask our claims department about that. They are the one who handles damages concerns.' The very next thing he said was that he probably won't book.
top_strength: Nicole's packing quote is the most complete pricing answer anyone gave this week, and she built it without being asked twice. The customer said 'I want a quote for just the move and then I would like a quote for if you guys were to pack as well,' and she came back with rate, materials, duration, and a downgrade path in one pass: 'if you will be adding packing service we charge the same hourly rate for packing service $202 per hour and we will bring all the materials necessary to pack your items. And we will charge you only for the materials. We use usually packing an entire two bedroom apartment it takes around five to six hours with approximately $220 worth of packing materials. But if you would be asking partial packing only then it's definitely lesser than that.' Same rate, only-what-we-use on materials, a real hours figure, and an explicit cheaper option — that is a customer who can now actually make a decision about packing. Her core estimate is also sound and, unusually for this sample, not padded: she gave the typical range first and then placed him inside it with named reasons — 'usually for a typical two bedroom apartment it takes around four and a half to six hours with two movers and one truck. In your case since you're moving from second floor apartment [to a] 2 story home with forty minutes drive time between location. I will estimate this to take five to six hours' — followed by the right caveat, that it is time-based and he pays only what he uses. Stated range, specific variables, landed inside the range, honest framing. That is the estimate-accuracy behavior the company is trying to get everyone to. Her probe questions are also well-built where she asks them: the box anchor is correct ('for a typical two bedroom apartment we usually expect to see around 25 to 35 boxes to move. Do you think you'll follow within that range?'), the heavy-item threshold is concrete ('anything heavy like, workout equipment safe or any items that for like more than 400 pounds?'), and she caught the elevator nuance the moment the customer raised it. She also read the room on pace: he told her at the top 'let's try and make a little bit faster than [that]' after she quoted ten to fifteen minutes, and she delivered the whole call in eight — and she apologized cleanly when she talked over him ('Okay, what were you about to say? Sorry to cut you off'), which is a small thing most reps skip.
coaching_note: This call was winnable and it was lost on one question. The customer's closing words were 'honestly, you guys are way more sense of other people I've talked to so we probably won't go with you but this was good information' — he liked the information, he liked her, and he still walked, and the moment it turned is visible in the transcript. He asked what repair actually means on a damaged nightstand, and the answer was 'Sorry I think I can ask our claims department about that. They are the one who handles damages concerns.' His stated reason for asking was already on the table — 'we've just had people scratch things and mess things up.' He was not testing her policy knowledge, he was asking whether Einstein makes it right. Deferring to another department at that exact moment reads as 'we don't handle this,' which is the opposite of the answer. The line she needed: 'Repair means we send someone out to fix it — a furniture repair tech for a scratch or a gouge, a drywall or floor repair for the house itself. If it can't be repaired we replace it at today's value, and if neither works we reimburse you. That's up to two thousand dollars a move, and it covers doors, floors and walls at both places, not just what's in the truck. Most movers give you sixty cents a pound, which on a nightstand is about eight dollars.' She had the right instinct one turn earlier — 'we are not by the pound. We are by how much worth the item is' is genuinely good — and then folded on the follow-up. This is a knowledge gap with a known fix, and it is worth confirming she has the claims language in hand before her next shift. Second, and structurally larger: two whole sections scored zero. The Clock section — 0/4 — means a customer was quoted up to $1,287 without ever being told when billing starts, that there is a two-and-a-half-hour minimum, or that time is prorated in fifteen-minute increments. Those are the questions every competitor will answer, and the absence reads as vagueness on the one thing a time-based company must be precise about. The Quote/Booking section — 0/11 — is worse: she has no email address. Eight minutes of discovery, a full quote, a packing quote, and there is no lead record and no way to follow up. When he said 'I'll reach out if we decide to go with you guys,' the answer was: 'Absolutely. Let me at least send this to you in writing so you've got our numbers next to everyone else's — what's the best email? And there's no deposit and nothing on a card to book, so if Sunday the twentieth is the day, I can hold it for you now at no cost and you can cancel by reply if you go another direction.' Third, she opened a price lever and dropped it. She told him rates vary by day and then never said which days are cheaper or by how much. If Sunday is a premium day and Tuesday through Thursday saves him real money on a five-to-six hour job, that is a hundred dollars he never got offered — and on a comparison-shopping call, the cheaper alternative is the thing that keeps you in the running. Fourth, he asked for two quotes, with and without the elevator, and got one. Answering exactly what a customer asked for is table stakes; skipping it on a customer who is explicitly benchmarking you against others is how you become the vendor with 'good information' that nobody books. Finally, use the name. She asked for it in her first sentence and never said 'Hunter' once.
phone_presence_notes: Courteous but almost entirely transactional — the probe ran as a checklist ('Okay. Awesome. How about any appliances... Okay, anything [valuable] or expensive, like, artworks'), the customer's name was never used across eight minutes, his one emotional disclosure ('we've just had people scratch things and mess things up') drew no acknowledgment at all, and when he pushed on what repair means the response was a handoff to another department rather than engagement; 'Okay, awesome' in reply to 'we probably won't go with you' is the clearest signal that the conversation was being processed rather than had.
audio_review_reason: Score of 2 triggers the rubric's automatic flag, and there are two specific things audio should settle. First, whether the flat read is real or an artifact of a sparse transcript — the customer asked her to speed up at the top and she compressed a fifteen-minute call into eight, so some of what reads as clipped may be her correctly following his instruction. Second, the rate delivery is garbled in a way the transcript cannot resolve: 'We charge $202 per hour for two movers and one truck. We pre $202,202,' immediately followed by the customer asking 'Is that one more time? How much?' — audio is needed to tell whether she genuinely stumbled over the central number of the call or whether the transcription mangled a clean delivery.
